extracted.intended_audience: early-17th-century English readers: potential colonists, investors, and policymakers interested in Virginia
extracted.subtask_description: A 17th-century pamphlet describing the condition, resources, and recent events (including a massacre) in the Virginia colony, together with a treatise on a Northwest passage and lists of benefactors and contributions. It is a promotional/informational tract aimed at encouraging settlement and investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of Virginia's climate and soil for settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Virginia is 'naturally rich, and exceedingly well watered, very temperate, and healthfull to the Inhabitants' and its situation 'betweenc the extremities of heate and colde' makes it capable of many commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites healthful air, moderate temperature, and fertile soil as reasons plants and livestock prosper; examples include successful growth of European plants, abundant grain, maize superior to English wheat, cattle and horses growing larger and stronger, does yielding multiple fawns, and plentiful fish and fowl. Used as an argument to attract settlers and investors by emphasizing longevity, fertility, and general suitability for English agriculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance and variety of natural commodities
rubrics_metrics.description: Virginia provides or promises many commodities: 'Furres, Cordage, and other Commodities; Masts, Plancks, and Boards, the Pitch and Tarre, the Pot-ashe and Sope-ashe, the Hempe and Flaxe... Iron... Wines, Fruits, and Salt... Silkes... Mulberry trees... Cotton-wooll, Silke-graffe and Sugar-Canes... Woods, Roots and Berries for Dyes; Plants and other Drugs; sweet Woods, Oyles and Gummes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet lists specific tradeable goods to show economic potential and to argue that goods now imported from Russia, Norway, France, Spain, Persia, Italy, etc., could be obtained from Virginia. Examples and claimed equivalence or superiority (e.g., mulberry for silk, maize superior to wheat) are used as evidence. This serves as a checklist for economic value when evaluating the colony's prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigability, harbours, and safe passage for trade
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'many therein being exceeding fayre and navigable' rivers and coasts, with 'faire and safe paflage thorow the maine Ocean'—no particular danger from pirates or rocks, and voyages that used to take months are now done in fewer weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet emphasizes numerous large navigable rivers, safe spacious harbours, and fewer navigational hazards to underline commercial viability and accessibility. It also cites reduced journey times and fewer losses at sea as evidence. These geographic/transport criteria are presented to reassure merchants and migrants about logistical feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic evidence supporting a Northwest passage
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a passage to the South Sea (Pacific) exists through the continent of Virginia (Fretum Hudson): rivers with heads in a ridge of hills running S–N that may connect to a western sea; reports that rivers flow into one great bay; tidal behavior at northern wintering points suggesting the Western Ocean is nearby; accounts from other discoverers (Hudson, Button) and native reports of seas to the west.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Henry Briggs' treatise and the main text list geographic indicators used to judge the likelihood of a northwest passage: mapped rivers and bays, mountain-ridge sources, tidal currents observed at wintering sites, comparative latitude/distance reasoning, and corroborating testimony from Indigenous peoples and other explorers. These are presented as criteria to evaluate prospects for opening a profitable western trade route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of local industries and infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of economic development: reports of iron-works, glass-works, salt-works, plentiful sowing of English grain, clearing of ground, planting of vines and mulberry trees, building of an inn in James-City, and stores of cattle and provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters from the Governor and Treasurer are cited to demonstrate concrete industrial progress; these features are used as measures of the colony's self-sufficiency and long-term viability. Presence of such works is offered as evidence to prospective settlers/investors that the colony supports manufacturing and public infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population and settlement growth metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting transports and settlers: '3370 People In the three laft yeares of 1619. 1620. and 1621... forty two Saile of fhips, three thousand fiue hundred and feauenty men and women for Plantation...' and 'fixty patents to particular persons' for plantations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet uses numbers of ships, passengers, mariners, patents granted, and the planting of new settlements as quantitative indicators of the colony's growth and momentum. These metrics are presented to reassure readers about robust immigration and organized colonization efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifications for conquest and dispossession after native treachery
rubrics_metrics.description: After recounting the massacre, the author enumerates reasons why the English may lawfully and prudently 'inva de the Country, and deftroy them': (1) betrayal of innocency will not go unpunished; (2) English hands previously restrained by forbearance are now freed to act; (3) commodities and game previously endangered by natives may be safely enjoyed by the English; (4) conquest is easier than civilizing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four enumerated arguments function as a moral/legal/political rubric presented to justify wartime reprisals, dispossession of land, and replacing native occupants with English settlers. They lay out criteria the author believes validate coercive measures following the massacre (divine justice, practical opportunity, economic advantage, and relative ease of conquest vs. civilizing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to native relations and 'civilizing' efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: The pamphlet discusses methods used to win native favor—gift-giving, building houses in English fashion, kind usage, lodging natives in planter houses, and religious teaching—as well as the risk that such trust may be repaid with treachery (example: Master George Thorpe's courtesies and subsequent murder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presents an evaluative tension: kindness and conversion are advanced as the civilizing policy but are shown to carry risks; the pamphlet thus offers an implicit criterion for strategy: balance benevolence with caution and preparedness. Examples show how over-familiarity and naïve trust are anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and charitable contributions as measures of metropolitan support
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of donations and benefactors (gifts of communion cups, plates, carpets, sums left in wills, funds towards schools, books for the college, and endowments) indicate metropolitan charitable support for the colony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet records charitable gifts, endowments, and bequests as evidence of English moral/religious investment in Virginia's institutions (church, college, free-school). These are presented as criteria signalling social legitimacy and long-term cultural aims for the plantation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisioning requirements for settlers (promised note)
rubrics_metrics.description: The title and preface promise 'a note of the charges of necessary prouisions fit for euery man that intends to goe to Virginia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the full detailed list is not present in the fetched text excerpt, the pamphlet signals that recommended provisions and associated costs are considered an important practical criterion for prospective settlers. The existence of such a note functions as a procedural checklist (provisions, stores, cattle, tools) that readers should consult before migrating.
